title: Bland W. Ballard of Tick Creek
summary: Bland W. Ballard scouted for George Rogers Clark and helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville, where raiders killed his family in 1788.
bodyMarkdown:
[Bland Williams Ballard](/people/#bland-ballard) was born in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, on October 16, 1761. He came to Kentucky in 1779, at seventeen. He would spend more than seventy years there as a scout, soldier, and lawmaker.

He scouted for [George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) on the 1780 campaign against the Shawnee towns north of the Ohio and again on the 1786 Wabash expedition. Scouts went ahead of the army, watched the trails, and carried word back. It was lonely, dangerous work, and a good scout had to know the woods better than the men he was watching for.

Around 1781 Ballard and [Robert Tyler](/people/#robert-tyler) planted Tyler Station on Tick Creek, east of present [Shelbyville](/stories/shelbyville/). It was one of a string of small, exposed stations in the Shelby County country between Louisville and the Bluegrass. Raids were common, and the [state marker for Ballard](https://history.ky.gov/markers/maj-bland-w-ballard) says he survived the Long Run and Tick Creek massacres and the Floyd's Fork ambush.

The worst came in October 1788. Delaware warriors attacked the family cabin near Tyler Station. The marker says Ballard's father, also named Bland, was killed with his wife and three children. The younger Bland fought back and killed six of the attackers, and two other children survived. Tyler Station was abandoned soon after.

Ballard kept fighting. He served with Anthony Wayne at Fallen Timbers in 1794, the battle that broke Native resistance in Ohio. In the War of 1812 he was wounded and taken prisoner at Frenchtown, in the [River Raisin defeat](/stories/river-raisin-1813-kentuckys-winter-defeat-in-michigan/) of January 1813.

Back home, Shelby County sent him to the General Assembly. He died in Shelby County on September 5, 1853, at ninety-one, one of the last of the frontier scouts. Kentucky named Ballard County and the town of Blandville for him, so his name now sits at the far western end of the state.

## Kentucky today

State historical marker #1088, "Maj. Bland W. Ballard," stands on US 60 at Cross Keys Road in Shelbyville. Its reverse side tells the Tick Creek massacre near Tyler Station, about three miles north. Ballard is buried in the State Cemetery at Frankfort Cemetery, near [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone)'s grave on the hill above the Kentucky River.
Source: [KHS marker #1088: Maj. Bland W. Ballard](https://history.ky.gov/markers/maj-bland-w-ballard)
